rows.why: Item 2 asks what unit the share is in and what its default is. The pick is basis points with a default of 7500. The run released 75 of a bounty of 100 and set 'partially released', so a bounty of 10000 releases 7500, which is what S1 expects.

Item 1 asks how an uneven share is rounded. The pick uses BigInt integer division, rounds down and gives the leftover to UAT. The run splitBounty(3, 5000) → {1, 2} shows that. So 999 at 7500 gives 749 and 250, and BigInt keeps it exact up to MAX_SAFE_INTEGER.
Item 8 asks how much UAT approval releases. The pick is the bounty minus earlier releases. The run released 90 after an earlier 10 and set 'fully released', which matches S3.
Item 7 asks what a failed run does and whether it saves. The run returned 'locked' with no releases. The single save it counted came from the later pass, so the failed run saved nothing.
Item 5 asks about UAT approval before the hidden tests pass. The run threw 'cannot release on UAT approval: the hidden tests have not passed', made 0 saves and left the state undefined.
Item 9 asks what a zero bounty does. The status is 'pro bono' as S6 expects, but the run recorded 0-amount releases for both events. S6 says no release is ever recorded.

Item 6 asks what a repeated event does. Duplicates are caught by release kind, so the same id or a different id of the same kind changes nothing. The run made 2 saves across 4 events and returned the unchanged state.

Item 11 asks how events that arrive at the same time are handled. The pick runs them one at a time through a promise queue. Combined with the check by release kind from item 6, two copies handled at once, with the same or different ids, record exactly one release.

Item 11 also asks whether an error blocks later events. The pick says a failed event rejects its own caller without blocking later ones. In the run the first call rejected with the store's 'boom' error, and since the set failed nothing was saved. A retry can then still succeed, though the run's output is cut off before showing it.
